title: Teodoro confident US would help PH if South China Sea tension escalates
summary: Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Monday expressed confidence that the US would honor its treaty commitments to the Philippines in case tensions escalate in the South China Sea.

blocks.text: Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Monday expressed confidence that the United States would honor its treaty commitments to the Philippines in case tensions escalate in the South China Sea (SCS).

“As of now, I have no reason to doubt. So it's a yes. But of course, that is conditioned on the fact that we don't do anything stupid, right?” Teodoro said at the Manila Dialogue on the South China Sea.
“I mean, we don't do anything that any country would object to, any right-minded and reasonable-minded country wouldn't object to. And that's vice versa,” he added.
Teodoro said the Philippines is also working with the US to prevent a potential clash in the SCS through stronger defense cooperation.
“We are here working together precisely on a defense basis to prevent the time when the time comes that, you know, the inevitable clash happens,” he said.
However, he said the Philippines would be more optimistic if there were a collective parity of potential force to serve as a backstop.
“I am optimistic. However, I will be more optimistic if there is a collective parity of potential force as a backstop. Anybody needs a backbone,” he said.

“If not, you have a wheelchair. So, even if you engage in anything, I think it's fundamental that we need a backbone. That backbone is resiliency. And unfortunately, as history has proved, a solid defense footing is really required for your national resilience,” he said.
Meanwhile, Teodoro said the Philippines cannot rely on China's goodwill in dealing with the proposed ASEAN-China Code of Conduct in the disputed waters.

"To see is to believe, and I will reserve my opinion on trust. I am not to rely on the good faith of an adversary. If I rely on the good faith of an adversary in my job as defense secretary, then they might as well find somebody else," he said.

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
Parts of the South China Sea that fall within Philippine territory have been renamed by the government as West Philippine Sea to reinforce the country’s claim.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago, including the Luzon Sea and the waters around, within, and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. — BM, GMA News
